Carol M. Bennett, PT
Sponsored
I treated neck thickening (forward head, collars that won't sit, the shape at the base) in Sweden for 20 years without handing out a single posture brace. When I moved to America, I couldn't believe what doctors here were telling their patients.

I've been a spine and rehabilitation specialist for 23 years. The first 21, I practiced in Sweden. I moved to the United States a little over two years ago, when my husband's hospital recruited him to Texas. I joined a good practice here. Good doctors. Good people.

And in my first three months, I saw something that kept me up at night. Women in their 60s and 70s coming in with a thickening at the base of the neck. Necks that had filled in where they used to taper. Heads sitting forward of the shoulders no matter how they tried to hold them. Some described feeling like their own outline had changed. Every one of them said the same thing. "My doctor says it's a dowager's hump. She's been managing it for years."

In Sweden, we do not manage this. We find what stopped holding the head, and we switch it back on. Because by the time someone is on a third corrector and being told to "learn to live with it," something has already been missed. And no strap fixes what was missed. It only holds the position.

Here's what your doctor probably hasn't told you about what a neck hump actually is.

Your neck does not thicken because the tissue at the back of your neck is broken. The muscles that hold your head up are not the ones you can feel.

They sit underneath. A deep layer running from the base of your skull down into your upper back.
Those muscles hold your head over your shoulders all day, without you ever thinking about them. When your brain is calling on them, your head sits where it should.

But here is what happens after 40.
Every hour your head sits forward of your shoulders, your brain calls on that deep layer a little less. Year after year, it answers a little slower. And as it goes quiet, the surface muscles take over a job they were never built to do.
Millimeter by millimeter, your head drifts forward and the tissue settles in around it.
Not damaged. Not caused by your posture alone. Switched off.

A muscle that has switched off does not hold. It gives way. It creates a head that drifts when nothing is pulling it, a collar that stands away when nothing has changed, a shape that grows while you are doing everything right.
Every sign of a dowager's hump. From a muscle that stopped, not one that died.

And that one word changes everything. Because tissue that has set may never go back. A muscle that has switched off can. You only have to switch it back on.

Your posture isn't the problem here. The protocol that treats the shape while ignoring the layer underneath is.

I want to be honest about braces, wedge pillows, and correctors. Because most of my American patients had been in them for years. Some using all three at once.
These products work on the outside. They hold your shoulders where you put them.
What they do not do is call on the muscle that stopped holding your head.
So the deep layer keeps going quieter. The shape keeps building. And your doctor keeps increasing the hours and telling you this is just how it is now.

A posture brace is like propping a sagging shelf while the bracket keeps working loose behind the wall. The shelf looks level. The bracket is still failing.
I have seen patients who came to me after 10 and 15 years in these products. Perfect compliance.

And every year, the shape had built a little further up the neck. Because nothing had changed at the layer underneath. As one of them told me, the braces never fixed what was wrong. They just changed what was wrong with her.

This is what nobody tells you about where this leads if the cause goes unaddressed.
It does not stay a fullness you cover with a collar.

The tissue settles. And settled tissue looks stable, so it feels safe. It is the most dangerous thing about this.

When tissue has settled long enough, it stops giving. Past that point it does not come back, no matter what switches on underneath it. That is the window closing, quietly, while you are being told to keep an eye on it.

And a woman who has stopped being photographed does not start again on her own. She stops standing side-on. Then she stops being in the frame. Then she stops going. That is how sociable, confident women end up spending their last good years at the edge of every room.
I have had that conversation more times than I should have. With women who did everything their doctor asked. Who wore every strap for 15 years. And still slowly lost their neckline, their photographs, and their confidence, because the cause kept advancing underneath, untouched.

When I arrived in the US, I assumed this research had simply crossed the ocean already.
In Sweden, rehabilitation specialists had been switching these deep muscles back on for over a decade. The work grew out of Scandinavian rehabilitation research, from specialists asking why some women recovered their head position and others, on the identical protocol, only got worse.

What they found was that the women who did not recover had measurable shutdown in the deep layer. The braces were holding necks whose own muscles were doing nothing. It was never a compliance problem. It was a signal problem.
A spinal rehabilitation institute in Sweden followed 540 women with so-called age-related neck thickening over 14 weeks. Two groups. Same guidance. One group also spent 20 minutes a day switching those deep muscles back on at home.

At 12 weeks, the first group kept getting worse.
In the second group, 91% had measurable reduction in forward head position. And 46% regained normal deep holding time on testing. The clinical marker for a muscle that has come back to life.

Independent of posture. Independent of exercise. It came down to the signal.

Since then, more than 21,500 women have used the at-home version of this. 91% reported visible change within the first weeks. 87% stopped wearing their brace entirely. 74% avoided a procedure they'd been told they needed.

I want to tell you about one patient, because her results are what I see when someone finally treats the right problem.

She was 66. A visible neck hump for five years. Three physical therapists. A brace and a wedge pillow used together. All three told her the change was permanent and to be careful about her photographs.

She almost didn't try. Five years of doing everything right had taught her not to hope. She said 20 minutes a day on a device could not undo what five years of straps hadn't.

I explained it simply. The brace was holding her shoulders. It was never designed to switch a muscle back on. Her neck was not broken. The layer holding her head had gone quiet, underneath, where no one had looked.

She agreed to try.
Week 2: the heaviness across her shoulders dropped from an 8 to about a 4. First time in five years it had gone down instead of up.
Week 3: she did her top button without checking the mirror first.
Week 6: standing in her own hallway, she caught her side profile in the glass and did not turn away. Actual recognition. She called her husband into the room and could not explain why she was crying.
Week 12: she asked her therapist to repeat the measurement. The numbers had improved. Not stabilized. Improved. She did not know what to say.

She had not worn the brace in three weeks. She had simply stopped needing the support.
Her husband told me quietly that he felt he had gotten his wife back. He had lost his companion to this too. Most spouses do, and no one ever asks how they are.
